claim: Three failed web logins PERMANENTLY disable EVERY web user account: status=0 is written to all WEBUSERS entries and nothing ever writes it back to 1.
corrected_claim: Three consecutive failed web logins against one *existing, currently-enabled* web username write status=0 into ALL FIVE WEBUSERS entries (plus accountLocked=1 for the offending user), and status==1 is a hard gate on web login, so every web account stops working. But this is NOT permanent and does NOT require rebuilding accounts: the touchscreen app writes status back to 1. tuxedo's CAccountsSetup screen (Settings -> user account setup) loads status from the file, renders each user's toggle button as "Enabled"/"Disabled" from it, offers per-user reset buttons plus an "Enable All" button, and on Apply writes status=1, accountLocked=0 and accLockedCount=0 for every row whose button does not read "Disabled" — then rewrites the encrypted JSON and notifies the web server. Usernames and passwords are repopulated from the file, so nothing has to be retyped. Correct statement: "three failed web logins disable every web account until someone clears it at the panel's touchscreen (Enable All / per-user Enable, then Apply)".
what_i_checked:
Static only; nothing run against hardware. Binaries: .../fw/carved/app2_root/opt/webserver/Barracuda and .../app2_root/tuxedo (both with intact .symtab). Custom capstone/pyelftools disassembler + literal-pool resolver + manual BL decoder (((w>>24)&0xF)==0xB, target=va+8+sext(w&0xFFFFFF)*4) in .../scratchpad/skept/{d.py,xr.py,litref.py,callers.py,fn.py}.

BARRACUDA (web server), the accusing side:
- updateLoginFailureCount @0x1537c. Loop 1 (i=0..4) finds the entry whose "userName" == submitted name, r6 = OLD atoi("accLockedCount"), writes accLockedCount=r6+1 and accLockedTime=time(). Then 0x15588 `cmp r6,#1 / ble 0x15634` — the lock block runs only when old>=2, i.e. on the 3rd failure. Loop 2 (0x15598-0x1562c) walks ALL FIVE entries: if that entry's accLockedCount==3 it sets accountLocked=1 (0x155dc-0x155f8), and then UNCONDITIONALLY falls through to 0x155fc-0x15620 which does json_pop_back(entry,"status"); json_delete; json_push_back(entry, json_new_i("status", 0)). So status=0 lands on every entry regardless of its own count. File is re-encrypted and written back (0x15644 /tmp/webuseraccountsenc.json -> 0x156bc -> /opt/tuxedo/configuration/webuseraccountsenc.json).
- The gate: readUserNamePasswordFromJSON @0x14bf8. Per entry: atoi("u8UserId")<=0 -> skip (0x14dc4); atoi("status") != 1 -> skip (0x14ddc/0x14dec). Only status==1 entries are ever compared against the submitted username. Called from MyUserDB_getPwd+0x54 (0x14f4c). checkTotalUserAccount @0x2c3f8 (0x2c594) and Invalid_html076EF::service @0x38604 (0x387e8) apply the same status==1 test.
- Trigger wiring: LoginTrackerIntf_LoginFailed_func @0x13a24 is the only caller of updateLoginFailureCount; it is installed as the LoginTracker interface at installVirtualDir+0x454 (pointer 0x13a24 at 0x149ec), and is reached from LoginTracker_loginFailed @0x651ec, whose only caller is FormAuthenticator_authenticate+0x56c (0x6615c). So it fires on ordinary form-login failures.
- Reset search, exhaustive: the string "status" exists exactly ONCE in Barracuda, at vaddr 0x8d768 (it is the tail of "Invalid parameter value for Thermostat mode status" — that is why a naive '\0status\0' scan finds nothing). I enumerated every 4-byte reference to 0x8d768 in all PT_LOAD segments: 5 hits, in readUserNamePasswordFromJSON, updateLoginFailureCount, checkTotalUserAccount, Invalid_html service, and WnmpDir_serviceField (the last is the door-lock API "status" = "open"/"close", unrelated — 0x2611c-0x26198). No other code in Barracuda can name that JSON key.
- resetLoginFailureCount1 @0x136d4 (called twice from authPage_service, 0x14290 and 0x14434, on an authenticated page load) clears ONLY accLockedCount, accLockedTime, accountLocked for the matching user — decoded 0x13878-0x138e0. resetLoginFailureCount @0x15074 is byte-for-byte the same behaviour and has ZERO callers and zero data references (dead code). Neither touches "status".
- No time-based unlock: xrefs to "accLockedTime" (0x85f08) are exactly 3, all in the three writers above; nothing reads it.

TUXEDO (touchscreen), the exculpating side — this is what the audit missed:
- createWebUserAccSetupJSONFile @0x439fa0 writes all 5 entries from a 0x64-stride struct array, including 0x43a044-0x43a058: json_new_i("status", *(u8*)(entry+0x52)). It is the only writer of the file besides migrateAccSetupFile.
- readWebUserAccSetupJSONFile @0x43acfc reads "status" back into entry+0x52 (0x43afe4 -> strb at 0x43b014); accountLocked->+0x53, accLockedCount->+0x60.
- CAccountsSetup::refreshScreen @0x32851c: 0x328664 `ldrb r3,[fp,#0x7a]` (= struct+0x52, since the struct array starts at this+0x28) -> non-zero sets the per-user button text to "Enabled" (0x328684), zero sets it to "Disabled" (0x3286e4). The same routine repopulates the username (this+0x29) and password (this+0x49) fields.
- CAccountsSetup::sltHandleUserResetAllPress @0x32c4f4 — the "Enable All" button (created at ctor 0x3293e8, stored at this+0x4c8): for each of the 5 buttons at this+0x4a0..0x4b0, if text=="Disabled" it setText("Enabled") (0x32c620-0x32c630) and decrements the disabled counter. Per-user equivalent: sltHandleUserResetPress @0x32c778.
- CAccountsSetup::saveuserDetailsInstruct @0x326fb4, the decisive instructions at 0x327588-0x3275fc: r7 = strcmp(buttonText,"Disabled"); if r7==0 -> `strb r6(0),[fp,#0x7a]` (status=0); if r7!=0 -> `strb r3(1),[fp,#0x7a]` (status=1), `str r6(0),[fp,#0x88]` (accLockedCount=0), `strb r6(0),[fp,#0x7b]` (accountLocked=0). This branch is reached for every non-empty user row on every Apply.
- CAccountsSetup::ApplySettings @0x327ee8 calls saveuserDetailsInstruct (0x327ef8), then createWebUserAccSetupJSONFile(this+0x28) at 0x327f40, then sync and sendUpdateCommandToWeb (0x327f58). sltHandleApplyPress @0x32830c drives it. CInitialAccountsSetup (0x4eedf4 / 0x4efd28 / 0x4f21a0) is the identical out-of-box-wizard copy.
- Callers of createWebUserAccSetupJSONFile: exactly 4 (migrateAccSetupFile 0x326a70, CAccountsSetup::ApplySettings, migrateAccSetupFileInit 0x4ee8b0, CInitialAccountsSetup::ApplySettings). References to the file path string 0x5ee7b0 in tuxedo: exactly 5, all inside those read/write/encode/presence helpers. Nothing in /etc/rc.d/init.d/startup or any rootfs script touches the file; `grep -rl webuseraccounts` over the whole rootfs matches only the two binaries.
why: The mechanism and the blast radius in the claim are real and I could not break them: the third failure does write status=0 to all five entries, and status==1 is a genuine precondition for a web account to be findable at login. What breaks is the word "permanently" and the consequence "until the accounts are rebuilt". The claim's own test — "decode every writer to that field" — was only applied to Barracuda. Barracuda indeed never writes status=1 (I proved that exhaustively: one literal, five xrefs, all decoded). But the field is a shared on-disk contract with the touchscreen app, and tuxedo's account-setup screen is a full read-modify-write of the same file: it renders status as the button label, exposes an "Enable All" button and per-user enable buttons specifically for this, and on Apply writes status=1 together with accountLocked=0 and accLockedCount=0. That is a live, shipped, user-reachable path, not dead code — unlike Barracuda's own resetLoginFailureCount @0x15074, which really is uncalled. Recovery is a panel visit, not an account rebuild; the usernames and passwords are reloaded from the same file and never have to be retyped.
preconditions:
All of these must hold on a real unit for the lockout to bite:
1. The web form login must actually be exercised. Remote/HTTPS access always authenticates; local LAN access only does if "Authentication for web server local access" is enabled on the panel (getLocalLoginStatus / setLoginForLocal / sltHandlLocalLoginChecked). With that box unchecked, LAN browsing never runs FormAuthenticator and cannot generate failures at all.
2. The typed username must exactly match an existing WEBUSERS entry (strcmp in updateLoginFailureCount loop 1). A wrong or unknown username increments nothing — r6 stays 0, `ble` is taken, the lock block never runs. So password-guessing against a bogus name is harmless; only mistyping the PASSWORD of a real account counts.
3. That entry must currently have status==1 (otherwise login already fails for a different reason).
4. The three failures must be consecutive for that username: any successful authenticated page load calls resetLoginFailureCount1 and zeroes that user's accLockedCount.
5. For recovery: physical access to the panel's touchscreen and to the Settings / user-account-setup screen. This is Lewis's own panel, so that holds.
Note the asymmetry that makes it feel permanent from the network side: once status=0, every subsequent web login attempt still matches the username in loop 1 (updateLoginFailureCount does not check status), so it keeps bumping the counter and re-writing status=0. There is no self-healing over time — accLockedTime is written by three functions and read by none — and no boot-time or script-based re-init.
owner_action:
Nothing to fix and nothing preventive to install. Two things worth knowing:

1. Recovery, if it ever happens: at the panel, go to the user account setup screen (Settings -> the screen with the User Id / User Name rows, the per-user Enabled/Disabled buttons and the "Enable All" button), press "Enable All" (or the individual user's Disabled button to flip it to Enabled), then Apply/Save. That writes status=1 and clears accountLocked and accLockedCount for every row showing Enabled, re-encrypts the file and tells the web server to reload. Do NOT press Apply while a row still reads "Disabled" — that path writes status=0 for that row. No usernames or passwords need re-entering; the screen reloads them from the file.

2. Operational caution for your own work: if you script, fuzz or replay against /login.shtml, three wrong passwords for a REAL username take the entire web interface offline for ALL five accounts until you walk to the panel. Do that testing only with the panel physically in reach. Guessing nonexistent usernames is safe.

If you want a belt-and-braces backup before poking at the login: copy /opt/tuxedo/configuration/webuseraccountsenc.json (and webuseraccountsenc_sec.json) off the unit first — but note it is AES-OFB encrypted and CRC-tracked in g_stCRC_data[0x10], so restoring it by hand is not a supported path; the touchscreen reset is the intended one.

claim: /opt/tuxedo/configuration/ is served over HTTP with NO authentication under a /Config/ URL, so panelinfo.txt (containing the INSTALLER CODE in plaintext) is one unauthenticated GET away.
what_i_checked:
Binaries: .../scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/opt/webserver/Barracuda (ARM ELF, intact .symtab, .text@0xc438, .rodata@0x84d30) and .../app2_root/tuxedo. No binutils on this box, so I used pyelftools + capstone with a manual 4-byte decode loop (own scripts under .../scratchpad/work/: strs.py, syms.py, xref.py, callers.py, darm.py).

1. DiskIo root. Literal xref on the string "/opt/tuxedo/configuration/" (.rodata va 0x86144) -> exactly one reference, installVirtualDir+0x4a0. Disassembled installVirtualDir (0x14598, 1208 bytes) in full:
  0x148d0 DiskIo_constructor(ioConfig.9297)
  0x148dc r1="/opt/tuxedo/configuration/"; 0x148e0 DiskIo_setRootDir  (failure -> baFatalEf, so if the dir is missing the whole server aborts)
  0x14914 r2="Config" (va 0x86160, also single-xref, installVirtualDir+0x4a8)
  0x14918 r0=readDir2.9296, r1=ioConfig, r3=0, [sp]=0 -> HttpResRdr_constructor
  0x14934 HttpServer_insertDir(server, r1=0, r2=readDir2)
 This block is the beq target of the allowVideoRecordingFromConfig test at 0x14800, i.e. it runs on both paths — unconditional.

2. Where it lands in the tree. HttpServer_insertDir (0x6e8ac) with parentName==NULL and a NON-empty dir name falls to 0x6e8fc -> HttpServer_createORGetFirstRootDir -> HttpDir_insertDir(thatRootDir, readDir2). HttpServer_createORGetFirstRootDir (0x6d760) returns *(server+0x68+0x10), i.e. the HEAD of the root list. HttpDir_insertDir (0x69b80) keeps that list sorted descending by the signed priority byte at +0x25. Insert order in installVirtualDir: insertCSP's DynHttpDir (prio 0, name ""), ehDir (prio 0, name ""), rootDir.9276 (prio 0, name ""), then highPrioRootDir.9277 at 0x147c0 = HttpDir_constructor(name=NULL, prio=1) -> becomes head. So by 0x14934 the head is highPrioRootDir, and "Config" is its child. VideoFiles and Videos land there too.

3. The authenticator. HttpDir_constructor (0x69f78) memsets the object to 0 over 0x28 bytes and writes only vptr, name(+0xc), prio(+0x25), list head(+0x20). HttpResRdr_constructor (0x72e8c) sets +0x28..+0x4c and never touches +0x14/+0x18. The only realm/authenticator objects in the image are realm.9273 (0x55b3b0) and fa.9289 (0x55b23c); xref says each is referenced from exactly one place, installVirtualDir, at 0x147b8/0x147bc:
  str r6,[r5,#0x18]  ; authenticator -> authenticateDir.9274
  str r8,[r5,#0x14]  ; realm         -> authenticateDir.9274
 r5 is authenticateDir, constructed at 0x147a8 with name "authenticated". readDir2 (0x55b1c4) and ioConfig (0x55b188) have no references anywhere outside installVirtualDir, so nothing patches them later.

4. HttpDir_authenticateAndAuthorize (0x6b544), decoded instruction by instruction:
  ldrh r3,[cmd,#0xb8]; if !=0 -> return 1
  ldrh r3,[cmd,#0xb6]; if !=0 -> return 1
  ldr  r3,[dir,#0x18]        ; authenticator
  if r3==0 -> 0x6b5ac: ldr r3,[dir,#0x14] (realm); if r3==0 -> mov r0,#1; return
 It reads only THIS dir's +0x14/+0x18. There is no parent walk, no server-level default, no fallback authenticator. Null authenticator AND null realm == return 1 == "serve".

5. Callers. Only three: HttpDir_doService+0x28, HttpResRdr_doService+0x30, EhDir_service+0xa0 — each passing its own dir as r0. Dispatch entry is HttpServer_processData+0xd60 -> HttpServer_serviceRequest(server, cmd, server+0x68, path) -> HttpServer_findAndExecDir -> baseDir->doService. I dumped every BL target of HttpServer_processData and HttpServer_executeCon: no session/login/tuxedo-specific call anywhere in the pipeline. So the only gate on /Config/<file> is readDir2's own null authenticator, plus highPrioRootDir's (also null, memset by HttpDir_constructor) and baseDir's (HttpServer_constructor never writes server+0x7c/+0x80).

6. Serving. HttpResRdr_doService (0x73718): after authenticateAndAuthorize returns 1, o->0x3c (extra filter) is 0 (set to 0 at 0x72ee8, never overwritten), the "/." traversal guard at 0x737b8 doesn't fire for a plain filename, and it falls to sendFile. mimeTypes table (0x54a8a0, 0x1b3 entries, walked programmatically) has txt -> text/plain, so no unknown-extension bail-out. DiskIo_mkAbsPath (0x5fd28) is literally rootDir concat name, DiskIo_openRes fopen "rb".

7. Listener. barracuda() at 0x10700 calls openSocketCon(server, disp, 0x50, 0x1bb, 1) then installVirtualDir(serverDB) at 0x1092c. In openSocketCon (0xc848) the flag==1 && port==0x50 branch builds the plain HttpServCon on port 80 unconditionally.

8. The payload. CreatePnlInfoFlashTable (tuxedo, 0x58f0a8) fprintf sequence read literally: "%s," GetPanelSoftwareVersion / "%d," GetSequenceNumber / "%d," GetHomePartition / "%s," GetPanelModel / "%d," GetTotalPartitions / "%d," GetTotalOutputs / then at 0x58f1b8: mov r0,#5; GetInstallerCode(5, buf); on success fprintf(f,"%s,",buf), on failure fputs("0000,",f) / then AuthLevelToEditSlotnRFZone, AllowedAuthorityFlag, ArmingModes, OpenCloseReporting, SingleKeyFireSilence, Hi/LoUserNumber, Hi/LoRFZoneNumber. Field 7 is the installer code. It is written to /tmp/panelinfo.txt, then 0x58f310 calls validateCRCFileOnFileWrite("/tmp/panelinfo.txt", "/opt/tuxedo/configuration/panelinfo.txt", ".../panelinfo_sec.txt") which (0x444fd4) is sprintf("cp %s %s") + system() twice, then "rm %s". Byte-for-byte plaintext copy, no encryption. GetInstallerCode (0x5951cc) is strncpy from gpmyPanel+0x52; that field is filled by myPanel::SetInstallerCode <- SetInstallerCode <- HandleInstallerCode (0x588140), which parses a CAL response from the alarm panel, requested by Apl_GetInstallerCode (0x584aec) via either Apl_SendNewCalMessage or Apl_SendOldCalMessage.

9. Corroboration that /Config/ is a live URL prefix: the shipped web app (.../scratchpad/webapp/script/getfilesrequest.js lines 924 and 1275) fetches "Config/cri_vidrec/ch"+ch+"/videofile_"+id+".mp4", and the Barracuda binary contains "rm -r /opt/tuxedo/configuration/cri_vidrec/*".
why:
I went looking for the four things that would kill this and found none of them.

- A parent authenticator: HttpDir_authenticateAndAuthorize does not walk parents. It is 35 instructions and reads exactly two fields of the single dir passed in. Both are zero for readDir2.
- A global default: there is no HttpServer-level authenticator field, no HttpServer_setAuthenticator symbol, and the only FormAuthenticator/SecurityRealm instances in the image are bound to one dir named "authenticated" and referenced nowhere else.
- Wrong subtree: I expected /Config/ might have been inserted under authenticateDir. It is not. insertDir with a NULL parent name plus a non-empty dir name resolves to the FIRST root dir, which by priority ordering is highPrioRootDir — the same dir authenticateDir hangs off, but as a SIBLING of it, not a child. highPrioRootDir itself is a bare memset HttpDir with no realm.
- A gate elsewhere in the request path: enumerated every call out of processData/executeCon/serviceRequest. Nothing.

The function-name assumption about panelinfo.txt also holds up when read as bytes: the 7th fprintf is fed by GetInstallerCode(5, buf) and the file reaches /opt/tuxedo/configuration/ via a shell `cp`, unmodified.

If anything the claim is understated in scope rather than overstated. The DiskIo root is the whole directory, so the same unauthenticated prefix also reaches panelinfo_sec.txt (identical copy), useraccountsetup.txt, webuseraccountsenc.json, Tuxedo.json, SystemConfig.txt, MailConf.txt, P<n>Info.txt, registereddevMAClist.json, zwavedevdb.json and hascenedb.json — all names hardcoded in the Barracuda binary, so no directory listing is needed to find them.

Two honest limits on what I can prove statically: I cannot show the file exists on a running unit, and I cannot show the installer-code field is non-"0000" on any particular panel. Both are preconditions below, not defects in the mechanism.
preconditions:
All of these are met on an ordinary commissioned unit, but they are what makes it actually bite:

1. Network reach to the Tuxedo's HTTP port. Port 80 plain HTTP is opened unconditionally at boot (barracuda+0x1bc), so this is LAN-adjacent by default. It becomes remote only if the unit is port-forwarded or on a flat network with untrusted devices. No TLS is required — HTTPS is a second listener, not a redirect.

2. No credentials, no session, no cookie needed. Verified in the bytes, not assumed.

3. The URL segment is case-sensitive: HttpDir_findDir (0x6a464) does strncmp against "Config". /config/ will 404.

4. /opt/tuxedo/configuration/panelinfo.txt must exist. It is written by CreatePnlInfoFlashTable, called from Apl_WaitTimerHandler+0x290 right after the panel-info exchange arms CurrentTimeTimer and PartitionStatusTimer. So it appears once the Tuxedo has completed an info sync with the connected Vista panel. A bench unit never paired to a panel will not have it (and DiskIo_setRootDir would still succeed, so you'd just get a 404).

5. Field 7 is the real code only if the panel actually returned it. GetInstallerCode reads gpmyPanel+0x52, populated by HandleInstallerCode from a CAL response. If gpmyPanel is NULL or the CAL exchange never completed, CreatePnlInfoFlashTable writes the literal "0000," instead. So on a panel/firmware combination that never answers the Get-Installer-Code CAL message, the field is a placeholder, not a secret. On a supported Vista paired normally, it is the live 4-digit installer code.

6. Nothing about physical access, a debug jumper, or a non-default setting is required. This is the shipped configuration of TUXW_V5.3.21.0.
owner_action:
Since this is your own unit, the definitive test is one command from another host on the same LAN — I did not run it, per the read-only scope:

  curl -sS http://<tuxedo-ip>/Config/panelinfo.txt

Expect a single CSV line. Count commas: field 7 is the installer code, or "0000" if your panel never answered the CAL request. Also worth checking on your unit: /Config/panelinfo_sec.txt, /Config/Tuxedo.json, /Config/useraccountsetup.txt, /Config/webuseraccountsenc.json.

If it returns the real code:

1. Treat the installer code as disclosed to anything that has ever been on that network segment. If the Tuxedo has ever been reachable from the internet (port 80 or 443 forwarded, UPnP, or a flat guest network), change it at the panel via installer programming and re-sync the Tuxedo.

2. Fix it at the network layer, because there is no firmware fix coming — 5.3.21.0 is the terminal release for Tuxedo Touch WIFI and the exposure is in the shipped installVirtualDir, not in a setting. Remove any port-forward to the panel, and put it on a VLAN/SSID that untrusted clients and IoT devices cannot reach. Do not rely on the web login: it protects /authenticated/, and /Config/ is a sibling of it, not a child.

3. If you are extending the firmware anyway, the one-line-equivalent fix is in installVirtualDir at 0x14934: insert readDir2 into authenticateDir instead of the root (HttpDir_insertDir(authenticateDir, readDir2)), or set readDir2+0x14/+0x18 to realm.9273/fa.9289 the way 0x147b8/0x147bc does for authenticateDir. Note that would also break the web app's own "Config/cri_vidrec/..." video fetches unless those requests carry the session, so test playback afterward.

What NOT to bother with: there is nothing to disable in the UI, and no configuration file that turns the /Config/ mapping off. It is created unconditionally at every boot.

claim: An EMPTY authtoken header short-circuits the REST API's HMAC comparison, branching past the entire MACID/HMAC build (claimed site ~0x00029c70 in Barracuda).
what_i_checked:
Binary: .../scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/opt/webserver/Barracuda (ELF32 ARM, .symtab intact). Disassembled with pyelftools+capstone, decoding B/BL manually and resolving every ldr-literal to its string.

- WnmpDir_service 0x29978..0x2a994 (whole function, incl. 0x29978-0x29b98, 0x29b80-0x29e00, 0x29e00-0x2a090, 0x2a780-0x2a828).
- Literal-pool resolution over 0x29978..0x2a994: the header name at 0x29c28, 0x29c74 and 0x29dc0 is the SAME string 0x0008eb24 = "authtoken"; error codes at 0x29c64/0x29de0/0x29df4 are 0x191 = 401.
- HttpRequest_getHeaderValue 0x6a360 (full).
- HTTP header parser inside HttpServer_processData 0x6fb8c..0x6fd00, plus HttpInData_extractLine 0x68e00.
- WnmpDir_serviceField entry 0x1eedc..0x1f160 and its error tail 0x28fe0..0x290a8.
- decrypt 0x1ccd0, handleErrors 0x1ccb4, Base64Decode/Encode syms.
- WnmpDir_constructor 0x1edec, HttpDir_constructor 0x69f78, HttpDir_doService 0x6cab8, HttpDir_authenticateAndAuthorize 0x6b544.
- installVirtualDir 0x14598 (gate at 0x14938-0x14950), allowSystemAPIFromConfig 0x318b4, getRegisteredDevNodes 0x188c8, callcheckforlocalremote 0x314b0 -> checkforlocalremote 0x2ddd0.
- Files: fw/carved/app2_root/root/Settings/WebConfig.conf; webapp/script/tuxapi.js lines 1-11 and 940-980.
Nothing was run against hardware.
why:
The mechanism is exactly as claimed, and I could not break it.

0x29c24: HttpRequest_getHeaderValue(req,"authtoken"); 0x29c30 cmp r0,#0; 0x29c34 bne 0x29c70; else 0x29c38 b 0x29df0 -> HttpResponse_sendError1(401). So an ABSENT header is 401.
0x29c70: the same call again; 0x29c7c ldrb r3,[r0]; 0x29c80 cmp r3,#0; 0x29c84 beq 0x29e2c. So a PRESENT-but-EMPTY value jumps straight to 0x29e2c, skipping 0x29c88-0x29dd8 entirely: the "MACID:"+DeviceMAC+",Path:"+url build, HMAC_CTX_init/HMAC_Init_ex(EVP_sha1, key=PrivateKey)/HMAC_Update/HMAC_Final, the %02x hexify loop, Base64Encode, and the strcmp.

Crucially, 0x29dd8 (the HMAC-matched branch) targets 0x29e2c as well - the identical address. So empty authtoken lands on the success continuation, not an error path. 0x29e2c re-reads getRegisteredDevNodes, re-finds the PrivateKey for the identity, and at 0x29ecc calls WnmpDir_serviceField - the real command dispatcher. It is a request-accepted path.

ABSENT vs EMPTY resolved at the parser, not by guesswork: getHeaderValue (0x6a360) returns 0 only when no name matches. The parser at 0x6fb98 does strchr(line,':'), NUL-terminates the name at the colon (0x6fbb0), then does a pre-indexed `ldrb r3,[sl,#1]!` loop skipping glibc _ISspace (0x2000). extractLine has already written a NUL at the CR. For "authtoken:\r\n" the value pointer therefore lands on that NUL - a valid pointer to "". So EMPTY -> non-NULL "" -> takes the bypass; ABSENT -> NULL -> 401. Both branches confirmed.

What does NOT survive is the implied consequence. This is not an authentication bypass:
1. Before the authtoken check ever runs, 0x29b50 requires an `identity` header (else 401 at 0x29c60), and the loop 0x29b94-0x29c50 requires it to strcmp-equal a "PublicKey" in /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json. No match -> 0x29c54 -> 401. identity is a 32-hex-char (128-bit) secret from the authenticated tuxedoapi.html page (tuxapi.js: api_iv_enc = readit.substring(64,96)).
2. WnmpDir_serviceField requires the `param` query parameter, Base64Decodes it and calls decrypt(0x1ccd0) = AES-256-CBC with key = 64 hex chars of PrivateKey and IV = the identity value. PrivateKey is the SAME secret the skipped HMAC was keyed with (0x29be4 strcpy to fp-0xba; 0x29d14 HMAC_Init_ex with that buffer). Anyone who could forge the HMAC already holds everything the empty-token trick grants, so no state-changing command becomes reachable that was not reachable before.

The real, narrower gain to an attacker is twofold: (a) it removes all binding of the request to (DeviceMAC, URL path), so a captured legitimate `param` ciphertext can be replayed against a different endpoint; and (b) it lets anyone holding only the identity/PublicKey reach decrypt() with arbitrary bytes - EVP_DecryptFinal_ex fails on the padding and handleErrors (0x1ccb4) calls abort(). That is a remote kill of the Barracuda webserver process, downgraded from "needs the 256-bit PrivateKey" to "needs the 128-bit PublicKey".
preconditions:
All of these must hold on a real unit:

1. The API must be enabled. installVirtualDir 0x14938 calls allowSystemAPIFromConfig and at 0x14940 SKIPS WnmpDir_constructor + HttpDir_insertDir entirely if it returns 0. That function reads /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf and strtok/atoi's the "Allow_API" line. The shipped default in this image is `Allow_API:01`, so /system_http_api IS mounted out of the box. Set it to 00 and none of this code exists at runtime.

2. The URL must NOT start with API_REV01/System, API_REV01/Administration or API_REV01/AutomationTest. Those three prefixes branch at 0x29aa8/0x29ac0/0x29ad8 to 0x29ed4, which uses callcheckforlocalremote (a crude 11-char peer-IP-vs-board-IP prefix compare at 0x2ddd0) and never touches authtoken. Everything else under /system_http_api is in scope: AdvancedSecurity/ArmWithCode, /Disarm, /DisarmWithCode, SetSecurityArm, SetDoorLock, SetGarageDoorStatus, ExecuteScene, SetLight, Registration/*, AdvancedMultimedia/*, etc.

3. At least one API client must already be registered - /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json must exist and parse. That file is NOT in the firmware image; it is created at runtime by Registration/Register. With no file, getRegisteredDevNodes returns {"Error":"File Pointer Is Null"}, 0x29b78 sees it and bails to 0x2a81c. A unit that has never had an API client enrolled is completely unreachable this way.

4. The attacker must know that client's PublicKey (the `identity` value, 32 hex chars). Without it: 401, always, before authtoken is ever read.

5. Request must be over HTTPS/443. For non-API_REV01/{System,Administration,AutomationTest} paths, 0x29a2c checks getRequestURL()[4]==':' (i.e. "http:") and answers with a 302 to https://<domain>:443/tuxedoapi.html at 0x29a8c, before any of the auth code.

6. Method must be POST - 0x29b1c requires req->0x44 == 0x10, else 405.

7. To actually change device state you additionally need the PrivateKey (64 hex chars) to build `param`. Without it you get an abort() of the webserver, not a command.
owner_action:
Concrete and proportionate for your own unit:

1. If you are not actively using the REST API, set `Allow_API:00` in /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf and reboot. That makes installVirtualDir skip WnmpDir_constructor at 0x14944 and the entire /system_http_api tree - and this whole code path - cease to exist. This is the one action that fully removes the issue; there is nothing to patch in the vendor binary.

2. Treat the `identity` / PublicKey value as a secret, not as a public one. It is the sole gate that stands between the network and decrypt(); and a wrong ciphertext there hits handleErrors -> abort() and kills the webserver until it is restarted. Do not paste it into scripts, gists or issue reports.

3. Do not port-forward 443 to the Tuxedo. Anyone who has ever seen the identity value can crash the web server at will. Keep it on the LAN / behind a VPN.

4. Prune registereddevMAClist.json - unregister API clients you no longer use (Registration/Unregister). Each live entry is one more PublicKey that unlocks step 2.

5. For your own interop tooling this is actually useful, and worth knowing deliberately: you can send `authtoken:` with an empty value and skip the HmacSHA1(\"MACID:<mac>,Path:<path>\", PrivateKey) step entirely. It will not get you in without the keys - you still need identity and a correctly AES-256-CBC-encrypted `param` - but it removes the MACID/path-binding step from your client, which is the fiddliest part to reproduce. Be aware you are relying on a defect, and that a firmware update could remove it.

6. Do not report this upstream as an "auth bypass". It is a request-integrity/binding defect plus a remote abort() DoS. Framed as an auth bypass it will be (correctly) rejected, because PrivateKey is still required for any command.

corrected_claim:
The dispatch mechanism is as described, but the scope and consequence are not. Accurate version:

(1) /handlerequest.html has no authorisation layer of any kind. The Barracuda dir it lives in has NULL authenticator and NULL authorizer, cspCheckCondition only filters HTTP methods, and the in-page gate is exactly: a (sessionid, tokenkey) pair that matches an entry in the sessItem table. Past that gate, every Type in the switch is reachable, and tuxedo's CReceiverThread::run dispatches MQ messages with no further checks. So "no per-command authorisation" SURVIVES.

(2) "Any valid session may arm/disarm" needs a qualifier. The web layer imposes nothing, but it only forwards uCode to the panel, which enforces it. Disarm (Type 3) always transmits the supplied code digits, so a session without a valid panel user code cannot disarm. Arm away/stay/night transmit no code when Quick Arm is enabled for the partition and uCode is 0 (Barracuda rewrites 0 to 0xffff, tuxedo then skips the digits) - so codeless arming is real, codeless disarming is not.

(3) There is no privilege boundary here to cross. Web accounts (max 5, in webuseraccountsenc.json) carry no role, authority or partition field at all - only name, password, id, status and lockout counters. So the absence of per-command authorisation is not privilege escalation between web users; it is simply that the product has one flat web privilege level and session+CSRF-token is the only gate.

(4) The "leftover demo data" characterisation is correct and in fact understated. securityDB is verbatim the Barracuda Application Server example table (family/dad, family/mom, family/kids, family) plus an empty-string catch-all, its role lookup MyUserDB_user2Roles is stubbed to return a constant 1, and MySecurityRealm_authorize has no reachable call site in the binary - it is stored into the realm object and never invoked by any code path. Even if it were invoked it would apply only to the "authenticated" dir, which contains one page (index.html), not handlerequest.html.

(5) The brief's premise is partly wrong: there is no GetUserAuthority in this firmware, and CUserAuthority::IsAuthorized / sltGoAuthLevelReceived gate only the touchscreen UI (and, for GoAuthLevel, merely relay the panel's answer). They never sit in front of a web command.
why:
I tried hard to find the check that would kill this claim and there isn't one. The three places it could live are all empty. Barracuda's own auth layer is not attached to the page: HttpServer_insertCSP puts handlerequest.html in the first root dir, whose authenticator/authorizer fields are NULL, so HttpDir_authenticateAndAuthorize returns allow immediately; the only dir carrying the FormAuthenticator and the realm is "authenticated", holding one page. The page's own preamble ends at a CSRF-token comparison and falls straight into a switch on Type with no table lookup, no role mask, no per-Type predicate. tuxedo's CReceiverThread::run reads the 0x194 message and calls the slot directly.

The authority machinery the brief pointed at is genuinely there but wired only to Qt screens: I enumerated every BL to CUserAuthority::IsAuthorized/Authority and every caller is a touchscreen widget class. sltGoAuthLevelReceived is on the web thread but is a reporter, not a gate - it converts the panel's per-partition response into VALID_USER_CODE/INVALID_USER_CODE for the browser.

The "demo data" claim I checked rather than repeated, and it holds on three independent grounds: the paths are the stock Barracuda example's, the role function is a constant-1 stub, and the authorize function is never called.

Where the claim overreaches is consequence. It reads as though a session buys you arm/disarm, and it does not buy you disarm: the code digits go to the ECP panel, which rejects an invalid code. And it implies a privilege boundary that this product does not have - the web user record has no authority field, so there is no lesser-privileged web account whose limits are being bypassed. That is why this is PARTLY_WRONG rather than SURVIVES.
preconditions:
For any of this to matter on a real unit, all of the following must hold:

1. An attacker must already hold a live (sessionid, tokenkey) pair from the sessItem table. Those are minted at login by the FormAuthenticator against webuseraccountsenc.json. Without them getCSRFToken1 returns NULL and the handler bails at 0x3e858/0x3e86c. So this is a post-authentication property, not an unauthenticated one.

2. The web/TotalConnect interface must be enabled and reachable, and no one must be logged in at the touchscreen in a way that sets localLoginStatus - if getLocalLoginStatus() or checkforlocalremote() is non-zero and the request carries no server-side session, the preamble denies at 0x3e85c.

3. For codeless arming specifically: gQuickArmState[partition-1] must equal 2, i.e. Quick Arm is enabled on that partition at the panel. With Quick Arm disabled, uCode=0 becomes 0xffff and the digits sent to the panel are garbage, which the panel rejects.

4. For disarm: a valid panel user code must be supplied in uCode. Nothing in the Tuxedo validates it, but the Vista panel does. No web session can disarm without knowing a real code.

5. The panel must be online (the JS checks hidPnlOnline, and the tuxedo side needs a working ECP/CAL path).

Note also that sessionid and tokenkey travel in the GET query string of /handlerequest.html, so they land in any proxy or server log in the path - that, not a missing ACL, is the realistic way a session token leaks.
owner_action:
Nothing to fix, and nothing to worry about on your own unit. There is no per-command authorisation to restore, because there was never a privilege model to enforce: the firmware supports up to five web accounts and they are all identical in power by design. The securityDB "ACL" is dead Barracuda sample code that is never executed - removing or correcting it would change no behaviour.

Two things worth taking away for the repair/interop work you are actually doing:

1. Treat /handlerequest.html as a flat command bus. Your tooling does not need to emulate any authority handshake - one valid (sessionid, tokenkey) pair reaches every Type. Type 1=arm away, 2=arm stay, 3=disarm, 4=arm night, and pID is a partition bitmask built from a strtok'd list, not a partition number. uCode=0 is rewritten to 0xffff meaning "no code"; that only works for arming, and only when Quick Arm is on for that partition. Disarm needs a real panel user code.

2. Operational hygiene, unchanged by this finding: keep the Tuxedo's web interface on the LAN and off any port-forward. The session id and CSRF token are carried in the URL query string, so a captured log line or referer is enough to replay any command - that is the exposure worth defending against, not the missing ACL.

If you want a genuine defence-in-depth change, the only one that would bite is network-level (VLAN/firewall the unit), not a firmware edit.

claim: The REST API AES-256 key and IV are a SINGLE GLOBAL PERMANENT device secret, generated once at first boot when the clock is hard-set to 01 Jan 2013 — not per session.
corrected_claim: The Tuxedo REST API uses one persistent AES-256-CBC key + fixed IV PER REGISTERED API IDENTITY, stored in /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json. The identity used by the web UI is literally named "Browser"; its key/IV pair is generated once, on the first Barracuda start that finds no "Browser" node, and is never rotated afterwards — not on reboot, not on login, not on session start. It is therefore permanent in practice, but it is not "the single global key": each device MAC enrolled via AddDeviceMAC gets its own independent pair (generateKeyForMAC), and those pairs ARE regenerable via the RevokeKeys admin endpoint (setrevokekeys). Both key and IV derive deterministically from srand(time(NULL)) — real entropy is the attacker's uncertainty about the one-second timestamp of generation, not 384 bits. The 01 Jan 2013 timestamp is the default-branch case (a genuinely virgin /opt/tuxedo/configuration), not a guarantee: the boot script only runs `date 0101000013` when /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime is absent, so a unit whose Browser node was first created after a firmware upgrade (datetime already present) is seeded from real wall-clock time instead.
what_i_checked:
All static, no device touched. Binaries: .../scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/opt/webserver/Barracuda and .../app2_root/tuxedo (both ARM32 ELF, intact .symtab; PT_LOAD maps vaddr = file offset + 0x8000). Tooling: pyelftools + capstone; whole-binary BL decode plus a literal-pool and MOVW/MOVT xref scanner, so I caught data references, not just names.

No session cookie, no username/password in that path.

No /etc/TZ, no /etc/localtime => UTC => time_t 1356998400. `settime` (the hwclock script) is NOT in cfg_services in /etc/rc.d/rc.conf, so no RTC read at boot. Barracuda is NOT started by startup (line 88 commented); it is started from CHomeScreen::sltInitHomeScreen @0x5b748-0x5b758 in tuxedo: apl_killProcess("Barracuda") then ui_sendMsgToSuperVisionThread(0xb, "/opt/webserver/Barracuda &"). I traced their consumers: MyUserDB_getPwd @0x14f3c (login-form password obfuscation) and the session identity sprintf("%d", getMyFreeIdentity()). None of them feed the REST payload crypto — that comes from the stored PrivateKey/PublicKey. So the "not per session" half of the claim holds.
SEPARATE FINDING the claim conflates — my_key_enc @0x55a6b4, my_iv_enc @0x55a6c4, my_key_enc_api @0x55a6d4, my_iv_enc_api @0x55a6e4, my_key_enc_scene @0x55a71c, my_iv_enc_scene @0x55a72c are all initialized .data hardcoded to 2b7e151628aed2a6abf7158809cf4f3c / 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f — the NIST SP 800-38A / FIPS-197 worked-example AES-128 key and IV. My xref scan found SIX references total, all read-only loads inside the six encrypt/decrypt wrappers; nothing writes them at runtime. Despite the name, my_key_enc_api is NOT the REST key: encryptAESforTuxdbAPI/decryptAESforTuxdbAPI (@0x1ee84/0x1ee20, AES-128-OFB) have ZERO callers and zero pointer references — dead code. my_key_enc IS live, via encryptAESforTuxdb/decryptAESforTuxdb, called from readUserNamePasswordFromJSON, resetLoginFailureCount, updateLoginFailureCount — i.e. the local web user-account store, protected by a firmware-universal textbook key.
why:
The mechanism in the claim is real and I could not break it. What I could break is its scope and its certainty.

What survives, hard: the key is not per-session (I chased the three genuine per-session key mechanisms to their consumers and none of them touch REST payload crypto); it is not regenerated on reboot or login (generateKeyForAPI runs every start but returns without writing once a "Browser" node exists); it is persisted to flash at /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json; and it is AES-256 + a fixed IV, matching the 64/32 hex split in tuxapi.js.

The entropy claim survives and is the real finding. random_string does srand(time(NULL)) then rand()%62 — glibc rand is fully deterministic given the seed, and EVP_BytesToKey runs with salt=NULL and count=1, so key AND IV together are a pure function of one 32-bit time_t. The ceiling is 32 bits, not the 384 bits the construction advertises. On a virgin first boot the seed is 1356998400 plus the seconds from the `date` line to the Barracuda start; that boot path is supervis, sleep 2, tuxedo, sleep 2, Qt init, home-screen init, kill+relaunch Barracuda — order tens to a few hundred seconds, so roughly 2^5 to 2^9 candidate keys. That is not weak, it is enumerable by hand.

It gets worse than the claim states, in a way worth naming: the IV is not merely fixed, it is the public lookup index. WnmpDir_service matches the cleartext `identity` header against each node's PublicKey. So a guessed seed is verifiable directly — derive key+IV, present the IV as `identity`, and the server tells you whether you guessed right. And the HMAC covers only "MACID:<mac>,Path:<path>", not the body and not any nonce, so a valid authtoken for an endpoint is a fixed string that replays forever. There is no session check on that path: the key IS the authentication.

Where the claim is wrong. "SINGLE" is wrong — registereddevMAClist.json holds one independent key/IV pair per identity; "Browser" is one entry, and every MAC enrolled through AddDeviceMAC gets its own pair from generateKeyForMAC. "PERMANENT" is right for the Browser pair (nothing rotates it automatically) but wrong as a blanket statement, because setrevokekeys regenerates a pair on demand. And "generated once at first boot when the clock is hard-set to 01 Jan 2013" states as fact something the code makes conditional twice over: `date 0101000013` is the else-branch of a test for /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime, and generateKeyForAPI writes only when the Browser node is missing. Those two conditions coincide on a factory-fresh config, which is the common case and probably what the analyst meant — but a unit that acquired its Browser node during a firmware upgrade, with datetime already on disk, was seeded from real wall-clock time. Same brokenness, different constant, and materially different for anyone trying to reproduce it on a specific unit.

One thing the analyst may have merged: there is a hardcoded key in this binary literally named my_key_enc_api, set to the NIST textbook AES-128 vector. It is not the REST key and it is dead code. Reasoning from that name alone would produce a claim that sounds like this one and is false. The claim as written points at generateKeyForAPI, which is the correct function — but the adjacent my_key_enc, same textbook constants, is live and does protect the local user-account file, and that one is identical on every unit running this firmware.

I cannot confirm from static analysis alone which seed Lewis's specific unit actually used. That is a fact about his device's history, not about the code, and it is settleable offline in minutes.
preconditions:
For the 2013-constant version to hold on a real unit, ALL of these must be true at the moment the Browser key was first created:
1. /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json contained no node with DeviceMAC == "Browser" — i.e. this was the first Barracuda start on firmware new enough to have generateKeyForAPI (present in 5.3.21.0), on a config partition that had never had one.
2. /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime did not exist at that boot, so startup took the `date 0101000013` branch. Both files live in the same directory, so a factory default or config wipe satisfies 1 and 2 together — that is why they usually coincide.
3. Internet time did not win the race: either GetOperationMode() <= 1, or the g_stDateTimeConfig[0x19] internet-time flag was clear, or the async NTP round trip had not completed before Barracuda called generateKeyForAPI. On a factory-fresh panel with no WiFi configured yet, this is automatic.
4. No RTC restored the clock — confirmed structurally: `settime`/hwclock is not in cfg_services, so nothing reads a hardware clock during boot.

For the weakness to be EXPLOITABLE rather than merely present:
5. The attacker needs network reach to Barracuda's HTTPS listener. Normal traffic is HTTPS (tuxapi.js hardcodes protocol="https"), so passive capture of an `identity` header requires TLS interception or local access — but note the attacker does not need to capture anything, because guessed seeds are verifiable directly against the server via the `identity` header.
6. Some endpoints are further restricted: WnmpDir_service calls checkforlocalremote/callcheckforlocalremote, and the AddDeviceMAC/RemoveDeviceMAC docs state LAN-only plus admin authorization. I did not enumerate which endpoints are LAN-gated, so the blast radius for a remote attacker is narrower than for one already on the LAN, by an amount I have not measured.
7. /tuxedoapi.html itself is NOT an unauthenticated key disclosure — it is gated by AuthenticatedUser_get1 and redirects to the login page otherwise. So the key does not simply fall out of the web root; the exposure is via seed brute force, not via reading that page anonymously.

What does NOT need to be true: nothing about session state, login timing, or reboots. The key is inert to all of them.

On his own unit Lewis already has the answer sitting in two places: /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json, and the page source of /tuxedoapi.html while logged in (the hidden `readit` input, first 64 hex = key, next 32 = IV). Take just the 32-hex PublicKey/IV. Then, offline, for seed s in range(1356998400, 1356998400+900): srand(s), take 31 chars of rand()%62 over "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ", run EVP_BytesToKey(aes-256-cbc, md5, salt=NULL, count=1), compare the derived IV to his. A hit proves the 2013 seeding on his hardware and hands him the exact key; no hit across that window means his Browser node was created post-upgrade with a real timestamp, and he should re-run the sweep across the plausible install window instead. This must be done with a glibc-compatible rand() — musl or Python's PRNG will not reproduce it.

Practical posture, and this is the part that actually matters: do not treat the REST AES layer as security. It is authentication, not just encryption — WnmpDir_service admits a request on the strength of the `identity`+`authtoken` pair alone, with no session, no body binding, and no nonce, so a valid authtoken replays indefinitely. Keep the Tuxedo off any port-forward and off the open internet, and put it on a segment where you would be comfortable with anyone who can reach it being able to drive the alarm API. That is a configuration change on his router/VLAN, not on the panel, and it is proportionate whether or not the seed turns out to be 2013.

Do not expect to fix this on the device. The key cannot be strengthened without replacing the generator, and forcing regeneration (wiping the config so a new Browser node is created) just re-runs the same srand(time(NULL)) — and if the clock is correct by then you get a real-timestamp seed, which is better than 2013 but still at most 32 bits. If he wants a materially better secret, the only route is a rebuilt Barracuda, which is a much larger undertaking than this finding warrants.

Two adjacent items worth folding into his notes rather than acting on now: (1) my_key_enc at 0x55a6b4 is the NIST textbook AES-128 key, identical on every unit with this firmware, and it protects the local web user-account store via encryptAESforTuxdb — that is a firmware-universal secret and arguably a worse one than the per-device REST key, though it needs filesystem access to exploit; (2) getKeyFromPassword @0x1d648 writes a NUL at out[31] after emitting 32 hex chars, truncating every session key it produces to 31 characters — a real bug, harmless-looking, but it means the session keys are a nibble shorter than intended.

claim: The REST authtoken is a STATIC per-endpoint value covering neither the request body nor any nonce, so capturing one lets it be replayed forever.
what_i_checked:

   - 0x29cec-0x29d44: HMAC_CTX_init, EVP_sha1, HMAC_Init_ex(key = the 64-char ASCII PrivateKey, keylen = strlen), exactly ONE HMAC_Update (0x29d2c) over that buffer, HMAC_Final. I grepped the whole function: one HMAC_Update, full stop.

2. Client side agrees: ...\scratchpad\webapp\script\tuxapi.js line 948 sets header "authtoken" = CryptoJS.HmacSHA1("MACID:Browser,Path:API_REV01/<endpoint>", api_key_enc) and header "identity" = api_iv_enc, for every one of ~40 endpoints.

Where the key comes from, and whether it rotates: tuxedoapi_html076EF::service @0x47ab0 fopen's /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json (@0x8b29c), finds the entry with DeviceMAC == "Browser" (@0x8b3d8) and emits `<input type="hidden" id="readit" value="%s%s">` = PrivateKey || PublicKey. tuxapi.js takes chars 0-63 as the HMAC key and 64-95 as the identity value. generateKeyForAPI @0x1d96c creates that entry (random_string(32) -> EVP_BytesToKey aes-256-cbc/md5 -> 32-byte key hex = PrivateKey, 16-byte IV hex = PublicKey) and is called exactly once, from barracuda+0x1b8 @0x108b8 at webserver start; at 0x1db4c it returns without writing if a "Browser" entry already exists. So the key is minted on first boot and then persisted, not per-login and not per-boot.

4. The cookie question (the thing that would have shrunk this to "life of a session"): WnmpDir_constructor @0x1edec calls HttpDir_constructor (which memsets the 0x28-byte HttpDir, leaving authenticator@+0x18 and realm@+0x14 NULL) then HttpDir_overloadService @0x69240, which literally does `ldr r3,[r0]; str r1,[r0]` - it replaces the dir's service pointer. The dir is inserted into the server's root dir (installVirtualDir 0x14950-0x14954), not under authenticateDir.9274 (the only dir that gets an authenticator, at 0x147b8/0x147bc). And grep of the full disassembly of WnmpDir_service (1031 lines) plus WnmpDir_serviceField @0x1eedc (43676 bytes, 10919 lines) finds ZERO references to HttpRequest_getSession, AuthenticatedUser_get1, "Cookie", checkforlocalremote or getRemoteAccess on this path.

5. Reachability gate: installVirtualDir @0x14938 calls allowSystemAPIFromConfig @0x318b4, which parses /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf for "Allow_API"; if 0 the WnmpDir is never constructed or inserted. The shipped file ...\app2_root\root\Settings\WebConfig.conf contains "Allow_API:01".
why:
I tried hard to break this and could not. The four things that would have refuted it all failed:
(a) "A session cookie is also required" - false. The API directory's service function is overloaded, which structurally bypasses Barracuda's per-directory authenticator, and neither the dispatcher nor the 43 KB field handler ever touches a session, cookie or AuthenticatedUser. The exposure is therefore worse than "for the life of that session", not better. (The login-protected page tuxedoapi.html is only how a human READS the key; it is not a gate on the API itself.)
(b) "The API is off in shipped config" - false. Allow_API:01 in the shipped WebConfig.conf.
(c) "Something else in the MAC input" - false. One HMAC_Update over a buffer built from three literals plus DeviceMAC plus path. Body, length and the tstamp field are not covered and tstamp is not even parsed server-side.
(d) "The key rotates" - false by default. Written once at first boot; generateKeyForAPI early-returns when the "Browser" entry exists. Only the explicit admin calls (setrevokekeys @0x19398, setAddDevMAC, setremoveMAC) or wiping /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json change it.

Two scope refinements, neither of which contradicts the claim:
- A replay needs the "identity" header too (the PublicKey), and the method must be POST ([req+0x44] == 0x10 checked at 0x29b20, else 405). Any captured browser request carries both, so this is bookkeeping, not a barrier.
- The token is per-(device, path). Same path always yields the same 40 hex chars for the life of the key; a token for /DisarmWithCode is useless for /ArmWithCode. Since the body is not covered, a replayer can also swap in a DIFFERENT ciphertext body for the same path - but forging a body that decrypts requires the PrivateKey, and anyone with the PrivateKey can mint every token anyway. So the realistic consequence of capturing one request is: indefinite exact replay of that one operation.

Two things I found alongside, flagged as untested and NOT part of the verdict:
- At 0x29c7c-0x29c84 the code fetches the authtoken header and, if its first byte is NUL, branches to 0x29e2c - the same "serve it" path taken after a successful compare - skipping HMAC verification entirely. Whether HttpRequest_getHeaderValue @0x6a360 can ever hand back an empty string for a header sent as "authtoken:" is something I cannot settle from bytes alone, and you told me not to touch hardware. Treat as a hypothesis, not a finding.
- Paths under API_REV01/System, API_REV01/Administration and API_REV01/AutomationTest (strncmp'd at 0x29a94-0x29ad8) skip the authtoken check completely and are gated only by checkforlocalremote @0x2ddo0, which compares the first three dotted octets of the peer IP against the board IP - a /24 heuristic. Those endpoints include the key-management calls. Same-subnet peers need no token at all for them.
preconditions:
All of these hold on a stock TUXW_V5.3.21.0 unit unless the owner changed something:
1. /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf contains Allow_API with a non-zero value (shipped: Allow_API:01). If it is 0, WnmpDir is never installed and every /system_http_api/... URL 404s - the finding cannot bite at all.
2. /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json exists and holds a DeviceMAC:"Browser" entry (created automatically at first webserver start).
3. The attacker holds a captured request to a path NOT under API_REV01/System|Administration|AutomationTest: the authtoken header, the identity header, the POST method, and the AES-encrypted param body. Capture requires a position that sees the plaintext HTTP - the page is served over TLS, so in practice: an intercepting proxy, a compromised or shared browser profile, a saved HAR/devtools log, or a MITM against a unit whose self-signed cert the user clicked through.
4. Network reach to the Barracuda listener (port from /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json). Unlike the System/Administration endpoints, the HMAC-protected endpoints have NO local-subnet restriction, so a port-forward or VPN-less remote exposure makes the replay reachable from anywhere.
5. Nobody has since called the revoke-keys endpoint, re-registered the Browser entry, deleted registereddevMAClist.json, or factory-reset the panel.

Note the alternative that makes capture unnecessary: any user who can log into the web UI once and view tuxedoapi.html reads the raw PrivateKey out of the `readit` hidden input and can then mint valid tokens for every endpoint, forever, with no further access.

Proportionate and concrete, in order:

1. Decide whether you actually use the REST API. If you do not, set Allow_API:00 in /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf (note the file uses CRLF line endings and colon-separated "Key:VV" pairs) and restart the webserver. That makes allowSystemAPIFromConfig return 0, WnmpDir is never constructed, and the whole surface returns 404. This is the one clean, verifiable mitigation available without rebuilding Barracuda.

2. If you do use it: treat the 64-hex-char "Browser" PrivateKey in /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json as a permanent, non-expiring bearer credential equivalent to the panel password - because that is exactly what it is. why:
The mechanism is real and I could not break it. Every one of the 25 page handlers routes through the same three-way flag, and when that flag lands on `getLocalLoginStatus()` returning 0 there is no `AuthenticatedUser` check, no HTTP auth (the FormAuthenticator is mounted only on `/authenticated`), and `MyPage_service` at `/redirect.html` will mint a session and a CSRF token for a caller that has presented nothing. The source address is the real socket peer, so it cannot be forged with a header, but nothing else stands in the way.

Three things in the claim are nevertheless wrong or overstated:

1. **"any host on the panel's /24"** — the test is `strcmp` of the first three dot-separated octets of two strings, with no reference to the interface netmask. On a genuine /24 that coincides. On a flat 192.168.0.0/16 or 10.0.0.0/8 it under-matches (same-subnet hosts are classed remote) and, conversely, a host on a *different* subnet that happens to share three octets is classed local. "Same first three octets as the panel's interface address" is the accurate statement.

2. **"gets full pages"** — not from the request it makes. A cookie-less GET of `/home.html` hits `cmp r7,#0 / cmpeq r5,#0` at 0x46134 and returns a 302 to `/redirect.html?url=home.html`. The page renders only on the second hop, after `MyPage_service` has created the session. Any browser or `requests.Session()` does this transparently; a single `curl` without `-L` and a cookie jar does not. The claim's outcome is right, its one-shot framing is not.

3. **Implied applicability to a shipped unit** — this is the part that most needs saying. `LocalLogin = 0` is not a default; it is a state a person has to choose. `addLocalLogin()` runs from `main()` on every boot of the `tuxedo` app and inserts `LocalLogin: 1` whenever the key is missing, and the settings checkbox only writes 0 behind an explicit "Authentication for local web server access will be disabled. Do you want to continue saving?" confirmation. So the honest reading is: **real code, high severity, but latent unless someone unticked the box.**

On the reconciliation — the integration's observation does **not** contradict this finding; the two touch disjoint code. `LocalLogin` gates only the CSP HTML pages (home, console, armcontrol, consolekeypad, mobileview, index, devicelist, …, plus `handlerequest.html`'s no-session branch and `MyPage_service`). It does not appear anywhere in the FormAuthenticator path, so `/authenticated/index.html` — the one credentialed login on the device — always demands a username and password no matter what the checkbox says. And it does not appear anywhere in `WnmpDir_service`, which serves the `/system_http_api/API_REV01/…` endpoints `ha-tuxedo-touch` actually uses (`GetSecurityStatus`, `AdvancedSecurity/ArmWithCode`, `AdvancedSecurity/DisarmWithCode`); that surface is gated by the `identity`-header / PublicKey registration on a separate `checkforlocalremote` test that never reads `localLoginStatus`. An integration whose first step is "log in" therefore sees exactly zero change when the box is unticked — which is what its docs reported. Both observations are true of the same firmware.

One secondary hazard the original analysis did not surface, which I would rate lower confidence but worth a line: `setLoginForLocal` writes the global on only two paths — fopen failure (→ 1, fail-closed) and a successful `BARRACUDA[0].LocalLogin` lookup. If Tuxedo.json exists and parses but lacks that key, the function returns having written nothing, and the global keeps its `.bss` value of **0** — fail-open. `addLocalLogin()` repairs the file, but it lives in a different process (`tuxedo`) from the reader (`Barracuda`, launched by `supervis`, which `startup` backgrounds first), so for that boot the panel would run open until an IPC msg 0x3e arrives — and that is only sent when someone toggles the checkbox. This only bites a unit whose config predates the key (e.g. an upgrade from a firmware without it), and I have no Tuxedo.json in the carve to say whether Lewis's is such a unit. It is a reason to verify the effective behaviour rather than trusting the file.

Absent that, `addLocalLogin()` has already written 1. (Or: the key is absent from a Tuxedo.json that otherwise parses, and Barracuda started before `tuxedo` repaired it — then the `.bss` 0 is in force for that boot.)

Both halves are confirmed in the shipped bytes, and the strongest counter-arguments do not hold.

The plaintext listener on port 80 is not conditional on anything. barracuda() calls openSocketCon(server, disp, 80, 443, 1) with no guard, and openSocketCon constructs an HttpServCon (cleartext) on 80 and an HttpSharkSslServCon on 443 in the same invocation, against the same HttpServer object. Port 80 and port 443 are open at the same time, always, and serve the same page tree. There is no setting that closes 80 — the HTTPS toggle only controls a redirect, and the "Barracuda port" setting only ADDS a second plaintext listener (default 6280 when unconfigured, plus TLS on 9443).

The uCode really is a GET query parameter carrying the raw 4-digit code. I verified it in the JS extracted from inside the firmware binary itself, and independently on the server side where handlerequest.html's service function calls HttpRequest_getParameter("uCode") and atoi's the result.

The one genuine mitigation I found, and its limit: index.html::service does bounce a cleartext request to https://<host>:<HTTPSExtPort>/redirect.html — but only when the HTTPS toggle is on, and ONLY from index.html. That toggle defaults to OFF (both binaries return 0 when the JSON key is absent, and no Tuxedo.json ships). So on an unconfigured or default unit the entire browser session, including every arm/disarm, runs over cleartext port 80. And even with the toggle ON, /handlerequest.html itself has no scheme check, so any client that goes straight to it — or to the documented /system_http_api/.../ArmWithCode?...&ucode= REST endpoint — on port 80 is served in the clear.

Second limit on the mitigation: the "HTTPS" here is the Real Time Logic SharkSSL "server demo 1024 bits" certificate compiled into the binary, valid 2009-08-27 to 2019-08-25. The private key ships in every copy of this firmware and the cert expired six years ago. Turning HTTPS on moves the code off cleartext but does not make it confidential against anyone on the LAN who has the firmware image.

So the claim survives as stated. The scope worth adding, which the original claim did not say: it is unconditional for the REST API and for any default-configured unit; for a browser session on a unit with the HTTPS toggle enabled the code rides TLS, but TLS backed by a published demo key.
preconditions:

2. Someone actually arms or disarms through the web UI (or the /system_http_api REST endpoint). If Lewis only ever uses the physical touchscreen, no uCode ever leaves the box and nothing here matters.
3. For the code to be in cleartext on the wire, one of:
   a. the "Secured web server access (HTTPS)" setting is off — this is the default state when /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json has no BARRACUDA[0].HTTPS key; or
   b. the client reaches /handlerequest.html or /system_http_api/... on port 80 directly rather than entering through index.html (a bookmark to an inner page, a script, curl, a mobile app, an integration).

4. Someone is positioned to see the packets. On a switched wired LAN with no port mirror and no ARP spoofing, that is nobody. It becomes real if: the Tuxedo or the browsing client is on Wi-Fi and someone else has the PSK (a guest, an ex-tenant, an installer); a router/AP/IDS/proxy on the path logs full URLs (many consumer routers' "parental controls" and Zeek/Suricata/pfSense setups do, for port 80 only); or port 80 is forwarded to the WAN.

why:
I tried to break this three ways and could not.

(a) "It's only a public cert, the key isn't really there." False. The 448 bytes after the DER are not padding: p*q reproduces the cert's own modulus exactly, and dP/dQ/qInv are mathematically consistent with e=65537. A working RSA private key, arithmetically verified, sits at file offset 0x0007d6b1 onward.

(b) "The key is there but something else serves the listener." False. SharkSsl_constructor is invoked exactly twice in 5.6 MB of code, both times in openSocketCon, both times with r2 = &sharkSslDemoCertSrv, and both immediately wire that SharkSsl into an HttpSharkSslServCon. There is no setCertificate API in the build, the PEM loader is unreachable dead code, and there is no key or cert file anywhere in the filesystem for anything to load. The demo credential is the only server credential that exists.

(c) "The path never runs on a shipped unit." False. supervis respawns Barracuda in a loop, and barracuda() creates the TLS listener unconditionally — no config key, no #ifdef, no runtime branch. Default is HTTP:80 + HTTPS:443; a non-80 configured port adds a second TLS listener on 9443. Both use the same demo cert.

So the claim is correct in mechanism and in scope. The only thing the audit did not state, and which changes what the finding is worth, is the consequence, which is conditional on the negotiated key exchange (see preconditions).
preconditions:
For the key to actually bite, on a real unit:

1. An attacker must be on-path: same LAN/Wi-Fi segment as the panel, or the panel's 80/443 (or configured port/9443) forwarded through the router to the Internet. The key by itself, held offline, does nothing.

2. For PASSIVE decryption of recorded traffic, the recorded session must have used a static-RSA key exchange. The server prefers DHE_RSA (suite list order 0x006b, 0x0039, 0x009e, 0x0067, 0x0033, 0x0016) and uses server preference, so a client that offers any DHE_RSA suite gets forward secrecy and the key does NOT decrypt that session — it only signed the ServerKeyExchange. But current browsers removed DHE years ago, so a modern Chrome/Firefox connecting here negotiates the first static-RSA suite the server matches (typically 0x0035 TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA, or 0x002f / 0x009c) — no forward secrecy, and the whole session is decryptable offline with the extracted key. Conversely, a browser new enough to have dropped TLS_RSA entirely cannot complete a handshake with this device at all (no ECDHE, no TLS 1.3 in this build), so there is nothing to record.

3. For SILENT impersonation, the client must trust this specific credential. Nothing does by default: the issuer is Real Time Logic's "demo CA" (not in any trust store), CN is "server demo 1024 bits" (name mismatch against any IP/hostname), and the cert EXPIRED 2019-08-25. Every browser already throws a full interstitial. That means an on-path attacker facing a user who clicks through warnings did not need the key at all — a self-signed cert would work equally well. The key adds genuine capability only against a client that pins this exact cert or the RTL demo CA. I found no such client in this firmware.

4. The plaintext HTTP listener on port 80 is always created regardless, and the HTTPS redirect only happens when the unit's "HTTPS enabled" setting is on in Tuxedo.json. If the owner browses over HTTP, TLS is not in the picture at all.

5. Not affected: the panel's outbound AlarmNet / Total Connect traffic. That goes through OpenSSL (lib/libcrypto.so.1.0.0) in the tuxedo/TotalConnect binaries, a completely separate code path that does not touch this key.

6. This is not a per-unit secret. It is baked into the firmware image, so it is identical on every Tuxedo Touch running TUXW_V5.3.21.0. The cert self-identifies as Real Time Logic's SharkSSL sample credential; if it is the same one shipped in the public SharkSSL/Barracuda SDK, the key is already public and "extracting from firmware" is not even required. I could not verify that against the SDK offline, so treat it as likely-but-unconfirmed.

There is no configuration fix. Barracuda has no code path that can load a replacement certificate or key — no setCertificate API, dead PEM loader, no cert file read. So do not go looking for a settings toggle; there isn't one.

Proportionate actions, in order:

1. Check the router: make sure nothing forwards 80, 443, 9443, or 6272 to the panel from the WAN. This is the single change that matters. An Internet-exposed panel turns a LAN-only issue into a remote one.

2. Treat the panel's web UI as non-confidential against anyone already on the same network. Put it on an isolated VLAN / guest-isolated SSID if convenient. If Lewis needs the UI from outside the house, reach it over a VPN into the LAN rather than exposing the port.

3. Do not assume the browser padlock means anything here — the warning it shows is accurate. Rotating the panel's user codes/passwords does not help against an on-path attacker who can decrypt the session and read them again.

4. Optional, and only if Lewis wants the project: the credential can in principle be replaced in-place. sharkSslDemoCertSrv is a fixed 1152-byte const blob at file offset 0x0007d3b1 whose internal layout is now fully known (693-byte DER, 0xFF pad, expLen/modLen/e header, n, p, q, dP, dQ, qInv, 64 bytes each). A freshly generated 1024-bit key plus a DER cert that happens to be <= 693 bytes could be assembled into the same footprint without relocating anything. That is a firmware-modification exercise with real bricking risk on a security panel, and it still would not produce a cert any client trusts. I would not do it for security benefit — only if he wants control of the key for his own pinned tooling.

Nothing here requires urgent action if the panel is LAN-only and not port-forwarded.

why:
The mechanism survives cleanly. The two setopt calls are not ambiguous: option 81 and option 64 are CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST and CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER, the value register r7 is provably 0 at both sites, and the surrounding option numbers (10002/10015/10001/20011) independently confirm the decoding because their argument registers hold exactly the URL buffer, the POST body pointer, the write-buffer struct and write_callback_func. There is no compensating check: curl is initialised in exactly one function, no CAINFO/CAPATH is ever set, and no CA store exists on the device.

What I could not sustain is the implied exposure. I went looking for a caller that never runs, and found something better than that: a state variable that gates the whole thing. thermostatclient does launch at boot on any unit whose Z-Wave module answers, so "it never starts" is not the refutation. But WifiThemroInitFunc reads the two credential files before the worker thread ever runs, and on a unit with no TCC account those fopen calls fail, config_get_username returns an empty buffer, and authState is set to -2. The worker loop's very first branch after a message-queue timeout tests exactly that value and goes back to sleep. Nothing in the boot-time message traffic from tuxedo can dislodge it: the only two commands that force a login (0x68, 0x6c) originate solely from the touchscreen setup screen, and the one command tuxedo does send at boot (0x67) is dispatched to PostStatusUpdatedMessage, which never touches curl — and even that is only sent when get_zw_devices.sh reports a non-zero device count.

I also downgraded the "Honeywell cloud host" framing on evidence rather than pedantry. nsloolup shells out to /dnshelper and substitutes a dotted quad into the URL, with a hard-coded 199.62.84.94 baked into .data as the fallback. Against an IP-literal URL, VERIFYHOST could never have passed, and with no CA bundle on the box VERIFYPEER could never have passed either. That reframes the finding from "someone disabled a check" to "this client was built with no way to authenticate the far end at all", which matters for what the owner should do about it.
preconditions:
For any of this to produce a single packet on a real unit, all of the following must hold:

1. The Z-Wave serial API must answer the version query in ZWaveInitNetwork (return 1 or 2 within 5 attempts). On a Tuxedo Touch WIFI with a working Z-Wave daughterboard this is satisfied and /thermostatclient is launched at every boot. If the Z-Wave module is dead or absent, the thread exits and the binary never runs.

2. BOTH /opt/tuxedo/configuration/thermostats/honeywell/username and .../password must exist and be non-empty. These are written only by the "Save" button on the touchscreen Wi-Fi Thermostat setup screen, i.e. only if the owner has linked a Total Connect Comfort account. With either file absent or empty, authState is pinned at -2 and the process idles on its message queue forever, making no TLS connection at all. Note that this is about the TCC *account*, not about whether any thermostat is currently paired — credentials alone are sufficient to start the login loop, and conversely a Z-Wave thermostat with no TCC account triggers nothing.

3. To actually be attacked, someone must be able to intercept the panel's traffic to the address /dnshelper resolves for tccaps.honeywell.com (default 199.62.84.94) — LAN position, ARP/DHCP/DNS control, or an upstream path. There is no pinning, no CA, and no hostname check, so any certificate is accepted and the attacker reads the plaintext TCC username and password out of the POST body and can forge every response.

Alternatively, condition 2 can be bypassed transiently by cmd 0x68/0x6c arriving on /Q_SendToWifiThermo, which forces an AuthenticateLogin with whatever (possibly empty) credentials are on disk. Those commands are only emitted by the touchscreen setup screen, so this still requires someone at the panel.
owner_action:
If no Total Connect Comfort account is linked on your unit — check read-only with `ls -l /opt/tuxedo/configuration/thermostats/honeywell/` (is `username` present and non-empty?) — then nothing. Do nothing. /thermostatclient is almost certainly running (`ps | grep thermostatclient` will show it), but it is parked at authState -2 and will never open a socket. Note it in your teardown as dormant, not as live exposure.

If credentials are present, or if you plan to link a TCC account: treat that traffic as unauthenticated plaintext-equivalent. The POST carries your TCC account password. Either don't link the account, or keep the panel on a network segment where you trust everything that can answer 199.62.84.94.

Do not "fix" this by patching the two setopt values to 1. That will break the feature outright rather than secure it: the URL is an IP literal so VERIFYHOST would fail every request, and there is no CA bundle anywhere in the rootfs so VERIFYPEER would fail too. A real fix means supplying a CA store, setting CURLOPT_CAINFO, and putting the hostname back in the URL (dropping the /dnshelper indirection or using CURLOPT_RESOLVE) — a substantially larger change, and one that is moot anyway since the TCC MobileV2 endpoint this targets has long since been retired. If you are extending the panel to talk to a thermostat service you control, write a new client rather than repairing this one.
